idiom_name: generator function as the unfold + functools.reduce (or an accumulator loop) as the fold
implementation_notes: A Python generator function is the coalgebra: its locals hold the seed, yield emits one layer, and the frame is suspended between elements, so nothing is materialized before the consumer asks for it. The fold half is functools.reduce(operation, iterable, initial) - or itertools.accumulate when the stream of partial results is wanted - and because generators are lazy, the two halves interleave in one pass: reduce pulls exactly as many items as it consumes. Build the list first (list(gen) or a comprehension) only when the values must be reused, indexed or consumed by several folds, since generators are single-use.
code_sketch:
import functools
import operator

def countdown(n):                    # coalgebra: unfold lazily
    while n > 0:
        yield n                          # suspends; state stays on the frame
        n -= 1

def factorial(n):
    return functools.reduce(operator.mul, countdown(n), 1)   # fused fold
pitfalls: A generator is exhausted after one pass: a second reduce over the same object silently returns the initial value, so hand out a fresh generator instead of a shared one.
functools.reduce without an initial value raises TypeError on an empty iterable; always pass the identity element, which the hylomorphism needs anyway for its terminal case.

Generators do not trampoline: a generator that recurses (or a generator comprehension nested deeply) still consumes the C stack, and an abandoned generator holds its frame until it is closed or collected.
